item.title: Business and Cities in the Global Economy
item.content:encoded:
Valeria Giacomin, Bocconi University

Youssef Cassis, European University Institute

Jan Logemann, University of Göttingen

Chinmay Tumbe, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad

This special issue examines cities as central agents in global capitalism and business expansion. Rather than treating cities as passive backdrops, the issue positions them as active institutional and infrastructural foundations that shaped how businesses, capital, and people circulated globally. The collection seeks to integrate perspectives from business history, urban history, and global studies to understand how cities mediated commerce, finance, manufacturing, and investment across regions and centuries.

Contributors are invited to explore how urban environments structured business globalization through various mechanisms: financial centers and trading networks, real estate and property investment, infrastructure development like ports and warehouses, informal and migrant-led trade circuits, and urban adaptation to crises and environmental change. The issue welcomes comparative work across world regions, with particular interest in underrepresented areas such as Japan, Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America, drawing on primary evidence and rigorous historical methodology.

Appel publié par Business History. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Cities as Nodes of Global Finance, Trade and Manufacturing: How did businesses use cities as hubs of commerce, credit, and investment in globalizing economies? What role did stock exchanges, banks, trading houses, and merchant guilds play in embedding global capital within specific urban contexts?
  • Cities, Real Estate, and Global Investment: How did property markets and urban real estate development become globalized? From colonial land concessions and foreign-owned plantations to the rise of multinational property firms, how did investment in land and real estate shape the growth, form, and business dynamics of cities?
  • Urban Infrastructures of Globalization: Ports, warehouses, transport corridors, and communication systems were often financed, managed, or operated by businesses. How did firms shape, invest in, and benefit from urban infrastructures that connected production and consumption across continents?
  • Migration, Informality, and Urban Globalization: How did informal markets, migrant entrepreneurs, and diasporic communities leverage urban density, mobility, and transnational connections to build alternative circuits of trade, credit, and labor?
  • Resilient Cities: Crisis, Adaptation, and Environmental Change: How did wars, revolutions, financial crises, pandemics, or deindustrialization reshape urban hierarchies? What does a long-term perspective reveal about the intertwined dynamics of crisis, resilience, and ecological transformation in shaping global urban capitalism?

Timeline

  • April 15, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • November 1, 2026: Manuscript deadline

item.title: Indigenous entrepreneurship under colonialism and beyond: institutional negotiation, exclusion and resilience
item.content:encoded:
Himadri Roy Chaudhuri, Xavier School of Business (XLRI)

Mark Tadajewski, University of York

Andrew Perchard, Otago Business School, University of Otago

Zoi Pittaki, University of Dundee School of Business

This special issue examines Indigenous entrepreneurial agency under colonial rule, treating colonial institutions as both economic constraints and sociopolitical structures that shaped market access, legal standing and accumulation strategies.

It invites business historical accounts of how entrepreneurs in colonised societies navigated, contested and reworked the rules of commerce, especially where access to courts, licensing, property rights, banking and credit markets was restricted or selectively enforced.

Contributions drawing on primary sources such as company records, court records, licensing files, banking archives, trading accounts, petitions, newspapers and vernacular-language materials are particularly encouraged.

Appel publié par Business History. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Entrepreneurship under legal and financial exclusion: responses to constraints in courts, licensing, taxation, banking, property rights, labour regimes and credit markets.
  • Institutional negotiation and boundary work: how entrepreneurial actors exploited institutional gaps, navigated plural legal orders, reinterpreted colonial rules and mobilised intermediaries or brokers.
  • Resilience as strategy: cooperative, mutual-aid and associational forms; diasporic, kinship and inter-regional networks; and late-colonial economic nationalism and early decolonisation as sites of institutional reconfiguration.
  • Innovation as resistance: technology adoption and adaptation through which entrepreneurs offered alternatives that subverted or circumvented colonial hegemony.
  • Comparative or connected histories that use the shared conceptual lens across cases.
  • Submissions may use archival research, oral history, biography, microhistory, and comparative or connected history, and may engage postcolonial scholarship, subaltern studies, and critical perspectives on firms, markets and institutions.

Timeline

  • October 1, 2026: Abstract deadline
  • May 1, 2027: Manuscript deadline
